blocks.body:
A number can be broken into smaller numbers, and smaller numbers can be put together to make it. Five toys can be split into 2 toys and 3 toys; 2 toys and 3 toys put together make 5 toys again. Putting together is called composing, and breaking apart is called decomposing. In England the pairs that make a number are called number bonds.

This page goes step by step: wholes and parts, how to draw and write a split, finding every way to split a number, finding a missing part, seeing 6 to 9 as five and some more, the pairs that make 10, the numbers 11 to 19 as ten and some more, and using these facts for numbers up to 20. It follows the Common Core standards for Kindergarten and Grade 1, the National Curriculum in England for Years 1 and 2, the Illustrative Mathematics lessons and the NCETM teaching materials.

You should already be able to count a group of objects and know that moving them around does not change how many there are (see [[counting-number-names]]). Each section starts with something to try, ends with exercises, and has notes for the adult helping.

blocks.title: Wholes and parts
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to split a group into two parts, put the parts back together, and say which is the whole and which are the parts.

Try this first. Take 6 cubes (or 6 buttons, or 6 pasta shapes). Hold some of them in your hand and put the rest on the table. How many are in your hand? How many are on the table? How many are there altogether? Now do it again, keeping a different number in your hand.

The whole group of 6 cubes is called the whole. The two smaller groups, the cubes in your hand and the cubes on the table, are called the parts. However you split them, the cubes in your hand and the cubes on the table together are still all 6 cubes.

blocks.caption: Left: one group of 5 squares. Right: the same 5 squares split into two parts, a part of 2 (blue) and a part of 3 (orange, striped). The whole is still 5.
blocks.alt: On the left, five empty squares in a row, labelled one group: 5. On the right, two blue squares labelled part: 2, a gap, and three orange striped squares labelled part: 3. Above the right-hand squares: whole: 5.

blocks.title: Whole and parts
blocks.body:
The whole is the complete group (or the complete object). A part is some of the whole. When a whole is split into parts, each part is smaller than the whole (unless the other part is empty), and the parts put back together make the whole again.

Examples: 6 cubes split into 4 in your hand and 2 on the table (whole 6, parts 4 and 2); a box of 5 eggs with 3 brown eggs and 2 white eggs (whole 5, parts 3 and 2).

Non-example: you have 6 cubes, keep 4 in your hand and put 1 on the table, and one cube rolls under the chair. The 4 and the 1 are not the two parts of 6, because part of the whole is missing; together they make only 5.

blocks.title: Composing and decomposing
blocks.body: Composing a number means putting parts together to make it: 2 and 3 compose 5. Decomposing a number means breaking it into parts: 5 can be decomposed into 2 and 3. Decomposing is also called partitioning or splitting.

blocks.title: The whole stays the same
blocks.body: However a group is split into two parts, the two parts together always make the same whole. Splitting 6 cubes as 4 and 2, or as 5 and 1, or as 3 and 3, still gives 6 cubes altogether.

When we split the group we only move cubes; we do not add any cube or take any cube away. Moving things around does not change how many there are (see [[counting-number-names]]). So if we count the cubes in the hand and then keep counting the cubes on the table, every cube is counted once, and the count ends at the same number as before. The bigger number has the smaller numbers inside it.

blocks.title: One split, many pictures
blocks.body: The same split, 5 as 2 and 3, can be shown in many ways. Children should meet several of them.

items.label: Objects
items.body: Put 5 cubes on the table. Push 2 to one side and 3 to the other. Say: 5 is 2 and 3.

items.label: Coloured dots
items.body: Draw 5 dots, 2 in one colour and 3 in another. A child can say: I know this is 5 because I can see 2 dots and 3 dots.

items.label: Fingers
items.body: Hold up 5 fingers on one hand: 2 fingers bent one way and 3 another, or 2 on one hand and 3 on the other.

items.label: Part-whole diagram
items.body: Write 5 in a circle at the top and 2 and 3 in two circles below, joined to it by lines (the cherry diagram, used in the next section).

items.label: Equation
items.body: Write $5 = 2 + 3$, read "five is two plus three".

blocks.title: For adults: say the whole every time
blocks.body: After each split, ask the child to say the parts and then the whole again: "3 in my hand, 3 on the table, 6 altogether." Illustrative Mathematics gives sentence frames for this as a support for children learning English: "I have ___ cubes in my hand. I have ___ cubes on my desk. I have ___ cubes altogether." Early years guidance asks adults to encourage children to say the whole that the parts make, and treats the idea that a total stays the same when its parts move as central to this work. So split, recombine and name the whole many times.
Diego has 4 cubes: 3 in one part and 1 in the other part. Lin has 4 cubes too: 2 in one part and 2 in the other. Do they have the same number of cubes?
blocks.solution:
1. Diego's parts are 3 and 1. Count them together: one, two, three, then four. Diego has 4 cubes.
2. Lin's parts are 2 and 2. Count them together: one, two, then three, four. Lin has 4 cubes.
3. Both have 4 cubes. The parts are different (3 and 1, or 2 and 2), but the whole is the same: 4 can be split in more than one way.

items.q: You split 7 cubes. 5 are in your hand. Are all 7 cubes still there, in two parts?
items.a: Yes. 5 are in your hand and the other 2 are on the table; together they are still 7.

items.q: In 8 = 6 + 2, which number is the whole?
Can a part be bigger than the whole?
items.a: No. Each part is some of the whole, so it is smaller than the whole (or, if the other part is 0, equal to it).

items.q: A plate has 6 grapes: 4 green and 2 red. What is the whole, and what are the parts?
items.hint: The whole is all the grapes.
items.solution: The whole is 6 grapes. The parts are 4 green grapes and 2 red grapes.

items.q: Put 5 cubes on the table and split them into two parts. Write down your two parts. Then find a different split.
items.hint: Push some cubes to one side and the rest to the other side.
items.solution: Any two of these: 1 and 4, 2 and 3, 3 and 2, 4 and 1 (and 0 and 5 if one side is empty). Each time the two parts make 5.

items.q: Sam had 7 cubes. He put 3 in a cup and 3 on the table. Is that a split of 7?
items.hint: Do 3 and 3 make 7?
items.solution: No. 3 and 3 make 6, not 7, so one cube is missing. A split of 7 into 3 and something must be 3 and 4.

items.q: Ana says: "I split 9 shells into two parts, and one part has 10 shells." Can she be right?
items.hint: Is a part smaller than the whole?
items.solution: No. A part is some of the whole, so a part of 9 shells cannot have 10 shells.

items.q: A box holds 6 eggs: some brown and some white. Tell two different stories about how many could be brown and how many white.
items.hint: The brown and white eggs together must make 6.
items.solution: For example: 1 brown and 5 white; or 3 brown and 3 white. Other answers: 2 and 4, 4 and 2, 5 and 1 (and 0 and 6, 6 and 0).

blocks.body:
- The whole is the complete group; the parts are smaller groups inside it.
- Composing puts parts together; decomposing (partitioning) breaks a whole into parts.
- However a group is split, the parts together make the same whole.
- The same number can be split in more than one way.
- A split can be shown with objects, dots, fingers, a diagram or an equation.

blocks.title: Drawing and writing a split
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to draw a split as a part-whole diagram or a bar model, and write it as an equation such as $7 = 4 + 3$.

Try this first. Make a tower of 7 cubes: 4 of one colour and 3 of another. Draw it. Now write the numbers 7, 4 and 3 somewhere on your drawing so that someone else can see which is the whole and which are the parts.

Two diagrams are used in many schools. The part-whole diagram (often called a cherry diagram, or a number bond diagram) has a circle for the whole joined by lines to a circle for each part. The bar model has a long bar for the whole and, under it, shorter bars for the parts, which together are exactly as long as the whole. Then we can write the same split with symbols.

blocks.caption: The split of 7 into 4 and 3, drawn two ways. Left: a part-whole (cherry) diagram, whole 7 at the top, parts 4 and 3 below. Right: a bar model; the bar for 7 is as long as the bars for 4 and 3 together. Both say 7 = 4 + 3.
blocks.alt: Left: a circle containing 7 at the top, joined by two lines to circles containing 4 (blue) and 3 (orange), labelled whole and part, part. Right: a long empty bar labelled 7 and whole; under it a blue bar labelled 4 and an orange striped bar labelled 3, labelled parts, together as long as the top bar. Below: 7 = 4 + 3.

blocks.title: Number bond
blocks.body: A number bond is a whole together with two parts that make it, such as 7 with 4 and 3. The number bonds of 5 are 0 and 5, 1 and 4, 2 and 3. The diagram that shows a number bond (the cherry diagram) is also called a number bond, or a part-whole model.

blocks.title: Plus, equals, expression and equation
blocks.body:
The sign $+$ is read "plus" (or "and"). It means the two numbers are put together: $4 + 3$ means 4 and 3 together. Something like $4 + 3$ is called an expression.

The sign $=$ is read "equals" or "is the same as". It sits between two things that are the same number. Writing $7 = 4 + 3$ says that 7 is the same number as 4 and 3 together. A statement with an equals sign, such as $7 = 4 + 3$, is called an equation (in some books a number sentence).

When we write a split, it is helpful to write the whole first: $7 = 4 + 3$ is read "seven is four plus three". The same fact can also be written with the whole last: $4 + 3 = 7$.

blocks.title: Swapping the parts gives the same bond
blocks.body: If 7 is 4 and 3, then 7 is also 3 and 4. So one number bond gives several equations: $$7 = 4 + 3, \quad 7 = 3 + 4,$$ $$4 + 3 = 7, \quad 3 + 4 = 7.$$

Take the tower of 7 cubes, 4 red and 3 blue, and turn it round. Now the 3 blue cubes come first and the 4 red cubes second. No cube was added or taken away, so it is still 7 cubes: 3 and 4 make 7 just as 4 and 3 do. (That adding in either order gives the same answer is a property of addition; see [[properties-of-operations]].)

blocks.title: Words for composing and decomposing
blocks.body: Different countries and books use different words for the same ideas.

rows.text: number bonds, for example "number bonds to 10 and 20"; splitting a number is called partitioning.
compose and decompose numbers; pairs written as equations such as 5 = 2 + 3; the number that makes 10 with another number.
make and break apart numbers; put together and take apart (for story problems).
composition of numbers; part-part-whole; the cherry diagram and the bar model.
number bond for the diagram; part and whole (total); number sentence for an equation.

Illustrative Mathematics and the Progressions write the total first: $10 = 7 + 3$, read "10 is 7 plus 3". England also writes the total last, and sometimes first, as in $9 + 7 = 16$, $16 - 7 = 9$ and $7 = 16 - 9$.

blocks.title: For adults: the equals sign does not mean "makes"
blocks.body: If children only ever see $4 + 3 = 7$, many come to think that $=$ means "and the answer is" or "makes". Writing splits with the whole first, $7 = 4 + 3$, helps them read $=$ as "is the same number as". Read both forms aloud and point out that each says the same thing. (More about this on [[equality-equal-sign]].)

blocks.title: For adults: the diagram shows everything at once
blocks.body: A finished part-whole diagram or bar model shows the whole and both parts at the same time, which some children find hard to take in. The Progressions suggest that moving between the whole and the parts makes it easier. So do not only show the finished picture: show the whole, then cover or separate it into the parts, and put the whole back together.
A tower has 8 cubes: 5 red cubes and 3 blue cubes. Draw a part-whole diagram and write two equations.
blocks.solution:
1. The whole is all the cubes: count them, 8.
2. The parts are the red cubes, 5, and the blue cubes, 3.
3. Draw a circle with 8 at the top. Draw two circles below it, write 5 in one and 3 in the other, and join each to the 8 with a line.
4. Write the whole first: $8 = 5 + 3$.
5. Check: 5 and 3 together, six, seven, eight. Yes, 8.
6. A second equation: $8 = 3 + 5$ (or $5 + 3 = 8$).

items.q: Write the split "9 is 6 and 3" as an equation with the whole first.
In a bar model, which bar is the longest?
Is $5 = 4 + 1$ the same number bond as $5 = 1 + 4$?
items.a: Yes: whole 5, parts 4 and 1, in a different order.

items.q: Read aloud: $6 = 2 + 4$. Which number is the whole?
items.hint: The whole is on its own on one side of the equals sign.
items.solution: "Six is two plus four." The whole is 6; the parts are 2 and 4.

items.q: A part-whole diagram has 10 at the top and 7 and 3 in the circles below. Write two equations for it.
items.hint: Start with the whole.

items.q: Draw a bar model for $5 = 1 + 4$.
items.hint: One long bar for the whole, and two shorter bars under it.
items.solution: A long bar labelled 5. Under it, a short bar labelled 1 and a longer bar labelled 4, side by side, together as long as the bar for 5.

items.q: Which of these is true: $7 = 5 + 2$, $7 = 4 + 2$, $7 = 6 + 1$?
items.hint: Do the two parts make 7? Count on from the first part.
items.solution: $7 = 5 + 2$ is true (5, then six, seven). $7 = 4 + 2$ is false (4 and 2 make 6). $7 = 6 + 1$ is true (6, then seven).

items.q: Write four equations for the bond with whole 9 and parts 5 and 4.
items.hint: Swap the parts, and write the whole first or last.

items.q: Elena colours 8 fingers blue and 2 red. Tyler colours 8 fingers red and 2 blue. Do their pictures show the same number bond?
items.hint: Look at the sizes of the parts, not the colours.
items.solution: Yes. Both show the whole 10 split into 8 and 2: $10 = 8 + 2$. Only the colours are swapped.

blocks.body:
- A number bond is a whole with two parts that make it.
- A part-whole (cherry) diagram puts the whole in one circle and each part in another, joined by lines.
- A bar model has a bar for the whole as long as the bars for the parts together.
- $=$ means "is the same number as"; $7 = 4 + 3$ is read "seven is four plus three".
- Swapping the parts gives the same bond: $7 = 4 + 3$ and $7 = 3 + 4$.

blocks.title: Finding all the ways
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to list every way to split a number into two parts, in an order that shows you have not missed any.

Try this first. Make a tower of 8 cubes, all one colour. Snap it into two pieces and write down the two numbers. Snap it back together and break it in a different place. How many different splits can you find? How do you know when you have found them all?

If we write the splits down in any old order, it is easy to miss one or to write one twice. A better way is to be systematic: start with the smallest first part and make the first part one bigger each time. Each step moves one cube from the second part to the first part, so the first part goes up by one and the second part goes down by one.

blocks.caption: All the ways to split 8 into a first part (plain blue) and a second part (orange, striped), in order: 0 + 8, 1 + 7, 2 + 6, 3 + 5, 4 + 4, 5 + 3, 6 + 2, 7 + 1, 8 + 0. There are 9 rows; in each row the first part has one more cube than in the row above.
blocks.alt: Nine rows of 8 squares, one under the other. In the top row all 8 squares are orange and striped, labelled 0 + 8. In each lower row one more square on the left is plain blue: 1 + 7, 2 + 6, 3 + 5, 4 + 4, 5 + 3, 6 + 2, 7 + 1, and in the bottom row all 8 are blue, labelled 8 + 0. This makes a staircase.

blocks.title: The ordered list has every split once
blocks.body:
To list all the ways to split a number into a first part and a second part, let the first part be 0, then 1, then 2, and so on, up to the whole number. Each first part has exactly one second part that goes with it. For 8 this gives 9 splits, from $0 + 8$ to $8 + 0$: one more split than the number itself.

If we count $4 + 3$ and $3 + 4$ as the same bond, there are fewer: the bonds of 8 are 0 and 8, 1 and 7, 2 and 6, 3 and 5, 4 and 4.

The first part can only be one of the numbers 0, 1, 2, and so on up to the whole (a part cannot be bigger than the whole). The ordered list tries each of these numbers once. For each first part there is only one second part: the number of cubes left over. So no split is missing and none appears twice. For 8 the first parts are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, which is nine numbers, so there are 9 splits.

blocks.title: For adults: how do you know you found them all?
blocks.body: Children usually find several splits by trial, in no order, and often miss one. In the Illustrative Mathematics lesson the class looks at cube towers of 8 split in two colours, writes an expression for each, and notices the pattern: one part goes up by one while the other goes down by one. Then they look for all the ways to break apart 7, and the teacher asks whether they found them all. The NCETM audit likewise asks teachers to develop a systematic approach to finding all possibilities. Ask "How do you know you have found all the ways?" and look together for the pattern.
Find all the ways to split 5 into two parts.
blocks.solution:
1. Start with 0 as the first part: $5 = 0 + 5$.
2. First part 1: $5 = 1 + 4$.
3. First part 2: $5 = 2 + 3$.
4. First part 3: $5 = 3 + 2$.
5. First part 4: $5 = 4 + 1$.
6. First part 5: $5 = 5 + 0$.
7. The first part cannot be bigger than 5, so we stop. There are 6 splits in order. If swapped parts count as the same bond, the bonds of 5 are 0 and 5, 1 and 4, 2 and 3.

blocks.body: Kiran has 7 pomegranates. Some go on the shelf and the rest go in the basket. How many could be on the shelf and how many in the basket? Give every answer that has at least one on the shelf and at least one in the basket.
blocks.solution:
1. This story has many answers: the whole, 7, is known, but neither part is.
2. Shelf 1: then 6 are in the basket. $7 = 1 + 6$.
3. Shelf 2: basket 5. $7 = 2 + 5$.
4. Shelf 3: basket 4. $7 = 3 + 4$.
5. Shelf 4: basket 3. $7 = 4 + 3$.
6. Shelf 5: basket 2. $7 = 5 + 2$.
7. Shelf 6: basket 1. $7 = 6 + 1$.
8. Shelf 7 would leave none in the basket, so we stop. There are 6 answers.

blocks.title: More than two parts
blocks.body: A number can also be split into three or more parts. Ten seeds can be shared among three pots, for example 3, 3 and 4; and 6 can be seen as 2, 2 and 2. Older children can split 17 in many ways, for example $17 = 10 + 7$, $17 = 11 + 6$ or $17 = 3 + 4 + 5 + 5$.

items.q: What split of 6 comes after $6 = 2 + 4$ in the ordered list?
How many ordered splits does 4 have, counting $0 + 4$ and $4 + 0$?
A list of the splits of 6 goes 1 + 5, 2 + 4, 4 + 2, 5 + 1. Which split with no 0 is missing?
List all the ways to split 4 into two parts, in order, starting with $0 + 4$.
items.hint: Make the first part one bigger each time.

items.q: List all the ways to split 7 into two parts that are not 0.
items.hint: Start with 1 as the first part and stop before the second part becomes 0.

items.q: Priya's list of the splits of 8 is: 1 + 7, 2 + 6, 3 + 5, 4 + 4, 5 + 3, 7 + 1. Which split with no 0 is missing?
items.hint: Look at the first parts: do they go 1, 2, 3, ... without a gap?
items.solution: The first parts are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, so 6 is missing. The missing split is $6 + 2$.

items.q: Without listing them, how many ordered splits does 10 have, from $0 + 10$ to $10 + 0$?
items.hint: The first part can be 0, 1, 2, ..., 10. How many numbers is that?
items.solution: The first part can be any of 0, 1, 2, ..., 10, which is 11 numbers. So there are 11 splits.

items.q: Write the bonds of 6, counting swapped parts as the same bond.
items.hint: Go up from 0 until the parts start to repeat in the other order.
items.solution: 0 and 6, 1 and 5, 2 and 4, 3 and 3. That is 4 bonds.

items.q: Split 9 into three parts in two different ways.
items.hint: Split 9 into two parts first, then split one of the parts again.
items.solution: For example $9 = 3 + 3 + 3$ and $9 = 5 + 2 + 2$ (also $9 = 1 + 4 + 4$, $9 = 6 + 2 + 1$, and others). Each time the three parts make 9.

items.q: Look at the splits of 8 with no 0 part: $1+7$, $2+6$, $3+5$, $4+4$, $5+3$, $6+2$, $7+1$. In which splits are both parts odd? In which are both even? (Odd and even numbers are on [[odd-even-numbers]].)
items.hint: The odd numbers are 1, 3, 5, 7; the even numbers are 2, 4, 6.
items.solution: Both odd: $1+7$, $3+5$, $5+3$, $7+1$. Both even: $2+6$, $4+4$, $6+2$. There is never one odd part and one even part, because 8 is even.

blocks.body:
- To find all the ways to split a number, start with the smallest first part and go up by one each time.
- Each step, one part goes up by one and the other goes down by one.
- In order from $0 + n$ to $n + 0$ there is one more split than the number $n$; 8 has 9.
- Counting swapped parts as the same, the bonds of 5 are 0 and 5, 1 and 4, 2 and 3.
- A number can also be split into three or more parts.

blocks.title: Know one part, find the other
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to find a missing part when you know the whole and the other part, and write the matching subtraction facts.

Try this first (a hiding game for two people). Put 7 small toys in a row and count them together. One person closes their eyes; the other hides some of the toys under a cup. Open your eyes: how many toys can you see? How many are hiding under the cup? Lift the cup to check.

If we know the whole and one part, the other part is fixed: it is the rest of the whole. We can find it by counting on from the part we know up to the whole, or by remembering the bond. This gives a new kind of equation, with a gap for the missing number, and it leads to subtraction.

blocks.caption: A bar model with a missing part. The whole is 9; one part is 6; the dashed bar with a question mark is the other part, which is 3.
blocks.alt: A long bar labelled 9 and whole. Under it, a blue bar labelled 6 and a dashed bar with a question mark, together as long as the top bar; labelled parts.

blocks.title: Missing part and subtraction
blocks.body:
A missing part can be written with a gap or a question mark: $9 = 6 + ?$ asks "9 is 6 and how many more?". The answer is 3.

The sign $-$ is read "minus" or "take away". $9 - 6$ means: start with 9 and take 6 away. Taking one part away from the whole leaves the other part, so $9 - 6 = 3$. Adding puts parts together into a whole; subtracting takes a part away from the whole.

blocks.title: One bond, four facts
blocks.body:
Every number bond with two different parts gives two addition facts and two subtraction facts. For the whole 9 with parts 6 and 3: $$6 + 3 = 9, \quad 3 + 6 = 9,$$ $$9 - 6 = 3, \quad 9 - 3 = 6.$$ The England curriculum also writes these with the answer first, for example $3 = 9 - 6$.

If the two parts are the same, as in $8 = 4 + 4$, there is one addition fact, $4 + 4 = 8$, and one subtraction fact, $8 - 4 = 4$.

Picture 9 cubes split into a part of 6 and a part of 3. Putting the parts together gives the whole, in either order: the two addition facts. Now start with all 9 and take the part of 6 away: what is left is exactly the other part, 3. Taking the part of 3 away instead leaves the part of 6. Nothing new has to be learned: the subtraction facts are the same bond read backwards.

blocks.title: Ways to find a missing part
blocks.body: Different sources show different ways to find the part we cannot see.

items.label: Hide and find
items.body: Hide some of a known number of toys, look at the rest, and work out how many are hidden; then lift the cover to check.

items.label: Fill the frame
items.body: A 10-frame is a box of 10 squares in two rows of five (it is explained in the next sections). Put some counters on it and find how many more fill it; the empty squares are the missing part.

items.label: Count on
items.body: Say the part you know, then count on to the whole, keeping track on fingers: 6, then seven, eight, nine, so 3 more.

items.label: Bar model
items.body: Draw the whole bar and the known part; the gap under the whole bar is the missing part.

items.label: Known bond
items.body: Remember the bond: if 6 and 3 make 9, then 9 is 6 and 3 more, and 9 take away 6 is 3.

blocks.title: For adults: the hidden part cannot be bigger than the whole
blocks.body: In hiding games a common mistake is to guess a hidden number that is bigger than the whole: 5 toys altogether, 2 still showing, and the child says 6 are hidden. Ask: "How many toys were there altogether? Could more than that be under the cup?" Encourage a sensible estimate first, then lift the cover and check.
There are 9 apples. 6 are on the table and the rest are in a bag. How many apples are in the bag? Write the addition and subtraction facts.
blocks.solution:
1. The whole is 9 apples. One part is 6 apples. The missing part is in the bag: $9 = 6 + ?$.
2. Count on from 6 up to 9, keeping track on fingers: seven (1 finger), eight (2 fingers), nine (3 fingers).
3. That is 3 more, so 3 apples are in the bag.
4. Facts: $9 = 6 + 3$, $9 = 3 + 6$, $9 - 6 = 3$, $9 - 3 = 6$.

items.q: You know $7 = 4 + 3$. What is $7 - 4$?
6 toys, 4 are showing. How many are hidden?

items.hint: Count on from 5 to 8.
items.solution: Six, seven, eight: 3 more. $8 = 5 + 3$, so the missing number is 3.

items.q: There are 6 birds. 1 is on the fence; the rest are in the tree. How many are in the tree?
items.hint: The whole is 6, one part is 1.
items.solution: $6 = 1 + 5$, so 5 birds are in the tree.

items.q: Write the four facts for the bond with whole 7 and parts 5 and 2.
items.hint: Two additions and two subtractions.
Which number and 4 make 9?
items.solution: $5 + 4 = 9$, so the missing number is 5.

items.q: Ben says: "10 counters altogether, 3 showing, so 13 are hidden." What would you say to him?
items.hint: Can a part be bigger than the whole?
items.solution: The hidden part must be smaller than 10. 3 and the hidden part make 10, so 7 are hidden: $10 = 3 + 7$.

items.q: Find the missing number: $9 - ? = 4$.
items.hint: 9 is 4 and how many more?
items.solution: $9 = 4 + 5$, so taking 5 away from 9 leaves 4. The missing number is 5.

blocks.body:
- If you know the whole and one part, the other part is the rest of the whole.
- Find it by counting on, by using a frame or bar model, or by remembering the bond.
- $-$ means take away; taking one part from the whole leaves the other part.
- One bond gives four facts, for example $6+3=9$, $3+6=9$, $9-6=3$, $9-3=6$.
- A hidden part can never be bigger than the whole.

blocks.title: Six to nine: five and some more
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to see each of the numbers 6, 7, 8 and 9 as five and some more, and ten as five and five.

Try this first. Hold up 7 fingers. How many fingers are on the full hand? How many on the other hand? Now show 8, then 9.

One full hand is 5 fingers. So 6 fingers are a full hand and 1 more, 7 fingers are a full hand and 2 more, and so on. Ten is two full hands: five and five. A 10-frame has a top row of 5 squares and a bottom row of 5, and we fill the top row first, so it shows the same thing. Seeing a number as five and a bit means we can see how many at a glance instead of counting one by one.

blocks.caption: 10-frames showing 6, 7, 8 and 9. The top row of each frame holds 5 counters (black); the extra counters (striped) are in the bottom row: 6 = 5 + 1, 7 = 5 + 2, 8 = 5 + 3, 9 = 5 + 4.
blocks.alt: Four 10-frames. Each has a full top row of 5 black counters. The bottom rows have 1, 2, 3 and 4 blue striped counters. Labels: 6 = 5 + 1, 7 = 5 + 2, 8 = 5 + 3, 9 = 5 + 4.

blocks.body: Count 7 counters into a 10-frame, filling the top row first. The first five counters fill the top row; the sixth and seventh go in the bottom row. So 7 counters are the 5 in the top row and 2 more. The same works for 6, 8 and 9: the top row always takes 5, and the rest go below. For 10 both rows are full: 5 and 5.

items.label: Fingers
items.body: A full hand of 5 and some fingers on the other hand: 8 is a full hand and 3 more.

items.label: 10-frame
items.body: A full top row of 5 and some counters in the bottom row.

items.label: Dot patterns and frames
items.body: Dots set out in a 5 and 2 pattern, or coloured 5 one way and the rest another way, so the 5 can be seen inside the number.

items.label: Number characters
items.body: In the children's programme Numberblocks, a number character can split into other number characters, which shows the smaller numbers inside it.

blocks.title: For adults: see the five, then count on
blocks.body: Encourage the child to see the full row (or full hand) as 5 straight away and then count on: "five, six, seven". Fingers can show the 5 and some more pattern, but ask the child to explain what they show. NCETM points out that seeing the 5 inside 6, 7, 8 and 9 is especially helpful, because relating numbers to 5 and to 10 supports efficient calculation later.
Show 9 on your fingers and say it as five and some more.
blocks.solution:
1. Hold up one full hand: that is 5.
2. On the other hand, count on: six, seven, eight, nine. That is 4 fingers.
3. So 9 is a full hand and 4 more: $9 = 5 + 4$.
4. Check: the other hand has just one finger down, so it shows 4.

items.q: 7 is five and how many more?
A 10-frame has a full top row and 3 counters in the bottom row. What number is it?
10 is five and how many more?
Write 6 as five and some more.
items.hint: Fill the top row of a 10-frame first.

items.q: A 10-frame has 5 counters in the top row and 4 in the bottom row. How many counters are there?
items.hint: See the 5, then count on.
items.solution: Five, then six, seven, eight, nine: 9 counters. $9 = 5 + 4$.

items.q: Draw 8 as a 10-frame. How many squares are empty?
items.hint: Top row full, then the rest in the bottom row.
items.solution: Top row 5 counters, bottom row 3 counters. The bottom row has 5 squares, so 2 are empty.

items.q: Mia holds up a full hand and 2 more fingers. Leo holds up a full hand and 4 more fingers. Who shows more, and how many does each show?
items.hint: Each full hand is 5.
items.solution: Mia shows $5 + 2 = 7$. Leo shows $5 + 4 = 9$. Leo shows more.

items.q: Use five and a bit to work out $5 + 3$ without counting from one.
items.hint: Five and three more.
items.solution: Five, then six, seven, eight: $5 + 3 = 8$.

blocks.body:
- One full hand, or one full row of a 10-frame, is 5.
- 6 to 9 are five and a bit: $6 = 5+1$, $7 = 5+2$, $8 = 5+3$, $9 = 5+4$.
- Ten is five and five.
- See the 5 at once, then count on.

blocks.title: Number bonds to 10
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to find, for any number from 1 to 9, the number that goes with it to make 10.

Try this first. Put 7 counters on an empty 10-frame. How many more counters do you need to fill it? Try again with 4 counters, then with 9.

A 10-frame has 10 squares. If some squares have counters, the empty squares show how many more are needed to make 10. The two numbers are partners: they go together to make 10. At first children count the empty squares; with practice they know the partner without counting. Ten is special: later, numbers are written in tens (see [[place-value]]), so these bonds are used again and again.

blocks.caption: Bonds to 10 on 10-frames. Black counters are one part; striped counters fill the rest of the frame: 10 = 9 + 1, 10 = 8 + 2, 10 = 7 + 3, 10 = 6 + 4, 10 = 5 + 5.
blocks.alt: Five full 10-frames side by side. The first has 9 black counters and 1 orange striped counter; the next 8 black and 2 striped; then 7 and 3; 6 and 4; 5 and 5. Labels underneath: 10 = 9 + 1, 10 = 8 + 2, 10 = 7 + 3, 10 = 6 + 4, 10 = 5 + 5.

blocks.title: The partners of 10
blocks.body: $$10 = 1 + 9 = 2 + 8 = 3 + 7$$ $$= 4 + 6 = 5 + 5.$$ Swapping the parts gives the rest: $9 + 1$, $8 + 2$, $7 + 3$, $6 + 4$. And $10 = 10 + 0$. So the partner of 1 is 9, of 2 is 8, of 3 is 7, of 4 is 6, of 5 is 5, of 6 is 4, of 7 is 3, of 8 is 2, and of 9 is 1.

Put a number of counters on a 10-frame, one in each square. The squares with counters and the empty squares together are all 10 squares of the frame. So the number of counters and the number of empty squares make 10: the empty squares are the partner. For 7 counters there are 3 empty squares, so 7 and 3 make 10.

blocks.title: Ways to see the bonds to 10

items.label: 10-frame
items.body: Fill a 10-frame with counters of two colours, or count the empty squares that are left.

items.label: Fingers
items.body: Show 10 fingers and colour or bend them in two groups, a different colour for each part: 6 fingers and 4 fingers.

items.label: Cube towers
items.body: Two towers, for example of 8 cubes and 2 cubes, that together have 10 cubes.

items.label: Shake and spill
items.body: Shake 10 two-colour counters in a cup and spill them; count each colour and tick the matching equation, such as $10 = 4 + 6$.

items.label: Equation
items.body: Write the partner with the whole first: $10 = 7 + 3$.

blocks.title: For adults: show two parts clearly
blocks.body: When asked to show $10 = 1 + 9$ on fingers, some children colour all ten fingers the same colour. Ask them to point to the 1 and to the 9, and to use one colour for each part. If a child matches a picture of 8 and 2 to the wrong equation, ask: "What two parts do you see? Does the equation show those parts?" Shake and Spill, with two-colour counters, is one of the games used for practice in these lessons.
What number goes with 4 to make 10?
blocks.solution:
1. Put 4 counters on an empty 10-frame: they fill 4 squares of the top row.
2. Count the empty squares: 1 in the top row, and 5 in the bottom row, so $1 + 5 = 6$.
3. So 4 and 6 make 10: $10 = 4 + 6$.
4. Check by counting on from 4: five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. That is 6 more.

items.q: What goes with 3 to make 10?
A 10-frame has 5 empty squares. How many counters are on it?

items.hint: How many empty squares on a 10-frame with 9 counters?
items.solution: 1 empty square, so $10 = 9 + 1$.

items.q: Find the partner of 6 to make 10.
items.hint: Count on from 6 to 10.
items.solution: Seven, eight, nine, ten: 4 more. $10 = 6 + 4$.

items.q: There are 10 children. 3 are inside; the rest are outside. How many are outside?
items.hint: Whole 10, one part 3.
items.solution: $10 = 3 + 7$, so 7 children are outside.

items.q: Jada spilled 10 counters. 5 landed red side up. How many are yellow?
items.hint: Every counter is red or yellow.
items.solution: $10 = 5 + 5$, so 5 are yellow.

items.q: What is $10 - 7$? Use a bond to 10.
items.hint: 7 and what make 10?
items.solution: $7 + 3 = 10$, so taking 7 from 10 leaves 3: $10 - 7 = 3$.

items.q: Which pairs make 10: 2 and 7, 4 and 6, 3 and 8, 5 and 5?
items.hint: Check each pair against the list of partners.
items.solution: 4 and 6, and 5 and 5, make 10. 2 and 7 make 9; 3 and 8 make 11.

items.q: Write all the bonds to 10 with two parts that are not 0, starting with $10 = 1 + 9$.
items.hint: The first part goes up by one each time.

blocks.body:
- The partners of 10 are 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5 (and 0 and 10).
- On a 10-frame the empty squares show the partner.
- Fingers, towers and counters show the same bonds.
- With practice, children know the partner without counting.

blocks.title: Teen numbers: ten and some more
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to see each number from 11 to 19 as ten and some more, and write it as an equation such as $14 = 10 + 4$.

Try this first. Fill a 10-frame with counters. Put 4 more counters next to it. How many counters are there? Did you need to count from one, or could you start at ten?

A full 10-frame is ten ones. The numbers 11 to 19 (the teen numbers) are ten ones and some more ones: 11 is ten and one, 12 is ten and two, up to 19, which is ten and nine. Because we already know the frame holds ten, we can count on from ten: eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen.

blocks.caption: A full 10-frame (10 black counters) and 4 more counters (striped) on a second frame: ten and 4 more is 14, so 14 = 10 + 4.
blocks.alt: Left: a full 10-frame of 10 black counters labelled ten. A plus sign. Right: a 10-frame with 4 blue striped counters in the top row, labelled 4 more. Below, in the middle: 14 = 10 + 4.

blocks.title: Teen numbers
blocks.body: The numbers 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 and 19 are made of ten ones and some further ones. We write this as an equation with the whole first: $18 = 10 + 8$ (eighteen is ten and eight). In Grade 1 the ten ones are seen as one ten, and 11 to 19 as a ten and some ones.

blocks.title: Ten and some more
blocks.body: $$11 = 10 + 1, \quad 12 = 10 + 2,$$ $$\ldots, \quad 19 = 10 + 9.$$ The second digit of a teen number tells how many ones there are as well as the ten. (Why the digits work this way is the subject of [[place-value]].)

Count 14 counters, putting the first ten into a 10-frame. After the tenth counter the frame is full. The counts eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen go with the counters outside the frame, so there are 4 of them. So 14 counters are the 10 in the frame and 4 more.

blocks.title: Fourteen says the four first
blocks.body: In English the teen words are irregular: "fourteen" says the four first, but the numeral 14 writes the 1 (for the ten) first. This makes ten and some more harder to see for English speakers, so it helps to say both: "fourteen is ten and four".

blocks.title: For adults: start at ten, not at one
blocks.body: Many children count every counter from one even when a full 10-frame is in front of them. Ask a child who counted on from ten to share how they did it, and ask: "When you counted, you started at 11. Why didn't you start at 1?" The answer we hope for: the frame is full, so there are already ten.
Write 17 as ten and some more, and show it with 10-frames.
blocks.solution:
1. Fill one 10-frame: that is 10.
2. Count on from ten until you reach seventeen: eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen. That is 7 more counters.
3. Put the 7 counters in a second frame: 5 in the top row and 2 in the bottom row.
4. So $17 = 10 + 7$.

items.q: A full 10-frame and 6 more counters. How many?
How many ones are there in 19 besides the ten?

items.hint: Count on from ten to fifteen.
items.solution: Eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen: 5 more. $15 = 10 + 5$.

items.q: What number is $10 + 8$?
items.hint: Start at ten and count on 8.

items.q: Show 12 with a full 10-frame and some counters. How many counters are outside the full frame?
items.hint: 12 is ten and how many more?
items.solution: $12 = 10 + 2$, so 2 counters are outside the full frame.

items.q: A child has a card with a full 10-frame. Which dot card, from 1 to 9 dots, should a partner bring to make 16?
items.hint: 16 is ten and how many?
items.solution: $16 = 10 + 6$, so the partner needs the card with 6 dots.

items.q: Write 11, 14 and 19 each as ten and some more.
items.hint: The second digit gives the ones.

items.q: Tom says: "Fourteen is four and ten, so I write 41." What is right?
items.hint: Which digit stands for the ten?
items.solution: Fourteen is ten and four, $14 = 10 + 4$, written 14: the 1 for the ten comes first. 41 is forty-one, a different number.

blocks.body:
- The teen numbers 11 to 19 are ten ones and some more ones.
- Write them with the whole first: $18 = 10 + 8$.
- With a full 10-frame, count on from ten instead of from one.
- English teen words say the ones first; the numeral writes the ten first.

blocks.title: Bonds within 20 and using a ten
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to use the bonds to 10 and the teen numbers to find bonds within 20, and to split a number so that it makes a ten.

Try this first. Put 8 counters on a 10-frame. You want to add 5 more. How many of the 5 fit in the frame? Where do the rest go? How many counters are there now?

The England curriculum asks children in Year 1 to know and use number bonds and the matching subtraction facts within 20, in several forms, and to know the bonds to 20 by the end of Year 2. The Common Core asks Grade 1 children to add and subtract within 20 using, among other ways, making ten. Both rest on the same facts from this page: the partners of 10, the splits of numbers below 10, and the teen numbers as ten and some more.

blocks.caption: Adding 8 and 5 by making a ten. The 8 black counters and 2 of the 5 striped counters fill the first frame (8 + 2 = 10); the other 3 striped counters go in the second frame. So 8 + 5 = 10 + 3 = 13.
blocks.alt: Two 10-frames. The first has 8 black counters and 2 blue striped counters, so it is full, labelled 8 + 2 = 10. The second has 3 blue striped counters, labelled 3 more.

blocks.title: Splitting to make a ten
blocks.body: To add a number to 8 (or 9, or 7), split the second number so that one part is the partner of the first number to make 10. For example, 5 is 2 and 3, and 8 and 2 make 10: $$8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3$$ $$= 10 + 3 = 13.$$ This needs three facts from this page: the partner of each number to make 10, the splits of numbers below 10, and the teen numbers as ten and some more.

Put the 8 counters and the 5 counters on two 10-frames, filling the first frame before the second. The first frame takes the 8 counters and then 2 more, because 8 and 2 make 10. Of the 5 counters, 2 went into the first frame, so 3 are left (5 is 2 and 3), and they go in the second frame. Now there is a full ten and 3 more, which is 13. No counter was added or lost, so $8 + 5 = 13$.

blocks.title: Bonds to 20 from bonds to 10
blocks.body: Each bond to 10 gives a bond to 20 by putting another ten with one of the parts. Since $3 + 7 = 10$: $$13 + 7 = 20, \quad 20 - 7 = 13.$$ Bonds within 20 come in several forms, for example $9 + 7 = 16$, $16 - 7 = 9$ and $7 = 16 - 9$.
$13$ is ten and 3. Adding 7 to the 3 makes another ten, because 3 and 7 make 10. So $13 + 7$ is ten and ten, which is 20. Taking 7 away from 20 undoes this and leaves 13.

blocks.title: Taking away across ten
blocks.body: To take a number away from a teen number, split the number you take away so that its first part brings you down to 10. For 14 - 6, split 6 as 4 and 2: $$14 - 6 = 14 - 4 - 2$$ $$= 10 - 2 = 8.$$ Check it with the bond: $8 + 6 = 14$, so $14 - 6 = 8$.

14 counters are a full 10-frame and 4 more. Taking away 6 counters is the same as taking away 4 and then 2 more, because 4 and 2 make 6. Taking away the 4 loose counters leaves the full ten. Taking away 2 more from the ten leaves 8. Every counter taken away is counted once, in the 4 or in the 2, so 6 are taken away in all.

blocks.caption: Taking 6 away from 14. The 14 counters are 4 loose ones (left frame) and a full frame of 10 (right frame). First the 4 loose counters (striped) are taken away, so 14 - 4 = 10. Then 2 more striped counters are taken from the full frame, leaving 8 plain counters: 10 - 2 = 8. In all 4 + 2 = 6 counters were taken away, so 14 - 6 = 8.
blocks.alt: Two 10-frames. The left frame has 4 orange striped counters in the top row (taken away first), labelled first: 14 - 4 = 10. The right frame is full: 8 black counters and 2 orange striped counters (taken away second), labelled then: 10 - 2 = 8.

blocks.title: For adults: making ten is one way among several
blocks.body: Children add within 20 in different ways: counting all, counting on, or composing a ten. The Progressions place making a ten among the methods in which a number is decomposed and part of it is composed with another number. It needs the partners of 10, the splits of small numbers and the teen numbers, so if one of these is shaky, practise it first. Taking away down to ten (the block above) can be harder than the forward methods, so counting up from the smaller number, as in the girls example, is also a good way. Compare methods together rather than insisting on one. (Addition and subtraction strategies are the subject of [[addition-subtraction]].)
Work out $9 + 4$ by making a ten.
blocks.solution:
1. 9 needs 1 more to make 10 (the partner of 9 is 1).
2. Split 4 into 1 and 3.
3. $9 + 1 = 10$.
4. Then $10 + 3 = 13$.
5. So $9 + 4 = 13$. In one line: $9 + 4 = 10 + 3 = 13$.

blocks.body: There are 16 children in a class. 7 are boys. How many are girls? Use a bond.
blocks.solution:
1. The whole is 16; one part is 7: $16 = 7 + ?$.
2. From 7, 3 more make 10 (the partner of 7 is 3).
3. From 10, 6 more make 16 (16 is ten and 6).
4. So the missing part is $3 + 6 = 9$.
5. $16 = 7 + 9$: there are 9 girls. Also $16 - 7 = 9$ and $9 + 7 = 16$.

blocks.body: Work out $14 - 6$ by taking away to ten.
blocks.solution:
1. 14 is ten and 4.
2. Split 6 into 4 and 2. Taking away the 4 brings us down to 10.
3. $14 - 4 = 10$.
4. Now take away the other 2: $10 - 2 = 8$.
5. So $14 - 6 = 14 - 4 - 2 = 8$.
6. Check with the bond: $8 + 6 = 14$ (8 and 2 make 10, then 4 more).

items.q: Which partner of 10 helps with $17 + 3$?
Work out $13 - 4$ by taking away to ten.

items.hint: 2 and 8 make 10.
items.solution: 12 is ten and 2; 2 and 8 make another ten. So $12 + 8 = 20$.

items.q: Work out $8 + 6$ by making a ten.
items.hint: Split 6 so that one part goes with 8 to make 10.

items.q: Work out $7 + 5$ by making a ten.
items.hint: The partner of 7 is 3.
15 and what make 20?
items.solution: 15 is ten and 5; 5 and 5 make another ten. So $15 + 5 = 20$ and $20 - 15 = 5$.

items.q: Write the four facts in the family of $9 + 7 = 16$.
items.hint: Swap the parts, then take each part away from 16.
From 9 to 10, then from 10 to 13.
items.solution: From 9, 1 more makes 10; from 10, 3 more make 13. So the missing part is $1 + 3 = 4$: $13 = 9 + 4$.

items.q: Work out $12 - 5$ by taking away to ten.
items.hint: Split 5 so that the first part takes you down to 10. 12 is ten and 2.

items.q: Work out $17 - 9$ by taking away to ten.
items.hint: 17 is ten and 7, so take away 7 first.

items.q: Find all the pairs of numbers from 0 to 20 that make 20 where the first number is 10 or more. How many are there?
items.hint: Start with $10 + 10$ and make the first number one bigger each time.

blocks.body:
- Bonds within 20 come from bonds to 10 and teen numbers: $13 + 7 = 20$ because $3 + 7 = 10$.
- To add across ten, split the second number to make a ten: $8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3 = 13$.
- This needs the partners of 10, the splits of small numbers, and teens as ten and some more.
- Every bond gives addition and subtraction facts in several forms.
- To take away across ten, split the number you take away so the first part brings you down to 10: $14 - 6 = 14 - 4 - 2 = 10 - 2 = 8$.

blocks.title: Looking ahead
blocks.body:
Splitting numbers into parts runs through all of school arithmetic. Seeing a teen number as ten and some ones is the first step of [[place-value]], where 324 is split as 300, 20 and 4, but can also be split in other ways such as 250, 70, 3 and 1. Bonds to 10 lead to bonds to 100 (since $3 + 7 = 10$, also $30 + 70 = 100$), and splitting to make a ten becomes a main tool of [[addition-subtraction]]. That swapping parts gives the same bond is the commutative law in [[properties-of-operations]], and missing-part equations such as $9 = 6 + ?$ are the first equations with an unknown ([[equality-equal-sign]]).

For older readers: a way of writing a number as a sum of parts, ignoring order, is called a partition, and counting partitions is a deep subject ([[partitions]]); for example 4 has five partitions, 4, 3 + 1, 2 + 2, 2 + 1 + 1 and 1 + 1 + 1 + 1. Asking which numbers can be made as sums of numbers from a given set is the study of [[additive-bases]], and [[generating-functions]] are a tool for counting the ways.
